questions.q: Which of these structures is pain-INSENSITIVE per the relevant-anatomy list?
questions.exp: Pain sensitive: dural venous sinuses, dura around vessels, large veins, circle of Willis, dural arteries (meningeal arteries), first few centimeters of medium sized vessels, pia mater, small cerebral vessels; pain insensitive: choroid plexus, ependyma. (Book p593)

questions.q: The primary headache causes listed in the classification are:
opts: Giant cell arteritis, SAH, brain tumour
Tension headache (m/c), migraine (2nd m/c), trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (e.g. cluster headache)
questions.exp: Classification: primary (benign, recurrent, no organic cause) - tension headache m/c, migraine 2nd m/c, TACs (eg cluster headache); secondary - systemic infection, brain tumour (rare). (Book p593)

questions.q: A new-onset headache after 55 years with scalp tenderness, thick/nodular vessels, jaw claudication, PUO and raised ESR points to which dangerous-headache cause?
questions.exp: Dangerous headache - new onset headache after 55 yrs: seen in giant cell arteritis, associated with scalp tenderness, thick/nodular vessels, jaw claudication, PUO, ESR raised. (Book p593)

questions.q: The raised-intracranial-tension features printed on the page include:
opts: Electric shock pain in V2 and V3 with triggers
Subacute, rapidly progressive over a few weeks, nocturnal awakening, vomiting preceding/relieving headache, intensity increased by bending/coughing (meningeal inflammation), blurring of vision
Chronic steady pain relieved by NSAIDs with no red flags
questions.exp: Up intracranial tension: subacute, rapidly progressive over a few weeks, nocturnal awakening, vomiting (precede/relieve headache), up intensity by bending/coughing (seen in meningeal inflammation), blurring of vision - do direct ophthalmoscopy, if papilledema (+) -> imaging (MRI, MRA, MRV). (Book p593)

questions.q: Papilledema found on direct ophthalmoscopy in this headache block triggers which investigation set per the page?
questions.exp: Investigation line for the raised-ICP/dangerous-headache block: MRI, MRA, MRV (after direct ophthalmoscopy; papilledema (+) -> imaging). (Book p593)

questions.q: Signs of raised ICP per the p594 list are:
questions.exp: Signs of up ICT: bradycardia, bradypnoea, hypertension, cardiac arrhythmia. (Book p594)

questions.q: The herniation complication line: the m/c herniation site and its sign are:
opts: Uncus (inferior part of temporal lobe) with 3rd nerve palsy
questions.exp: Complication: herniation -> coning -> death; m/c site: uncus (inferior part of temporal lobe); signs: 3rd nerve palsy; Rx: decompression. (Book p594)

questions.q: Middle-aged female, holocranial band-like pressure, ADL preserved, one-third with depression - which headache, and its chronic prophylaxis per the page?
opts: Tension-type headache; amitriptyline (TCA) d/t associated depression
questions.exp: Tension type headache (TTH): middle-aged female; 1/3rd cases associated with depression; holocranial band-like or pressure sensation; does not affect activities of daily living; no danger signs. Mx: acute NSAIDs; chronic amitriptyline (TCA) d/t associated depression (prophylactic). (Book p594)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the feature AGAINST tension-type headache per the page:
opts: No effect on activities of daily living
questions.exp: Against TTH: vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, aggravated by movement. (Book p594)

questions.q: The migraine feature list on this page includes which items?
opts: Continuous for months, onset after 55, M > F
Pulsatile pain with V2/V3 cutaneous triggers
Orthostatic, daily, bilateral, worse in morning
Episodic, adolescence onset, severity increases with age, F > m, family history +, normal systemic examination
questions.exp: Migraine features: episodic; adolescence onset; severity up with age; F > m; family history +; not attributable to other diseases; normal systemic examination. (Book p594)

questions.q: The migraine type split printed is:
opts: Common 80% (not associated with aura) and classical 20% (associated with aura)
questions.exp: Types: common (80%) - not associated with aura; classical (20%) - associated with aura. (Book p594)

questions.q: Aura duration per the classical-migraine line is, and the m/c visual phenomenon is:
opts: 15 minutes - 1 hour; fortification spectra (zig-zag lines in peripheral vision, hazy central spot)
questions.exp: Aura: subjective, duration 15 mins - 1 hr; visual (m/c) - fortification spectra (m/c): zig-zag lines in peripheral vision, hazy spot in centre of vision; sensory (tingling and numbness); auditory; motor. (Book p594)

questions.q: The stages of migraine on this page run in which order?
questions.exp: Stages of migraine: 1. prodrome -> 2. aura (zig-zag lines m/c) -> 3. headache -> 4. postdrome (lethargy, low mood/depressed). (Book p595)

questions.q: The prodrome and headache stages carry which features per the page?
opts: Prodrome: photopsia; headache: pulsatile with V2/V3 triggers
Prodrome: lethargy; headache: orthostatic and daily
Prodrome: visual scotoma; headache: 24-48 hrs constant

Prodrome: mood disturbance, irritability, depressive symptoms; headache: unilateral -> holocranial, frontotemporal, throbbing/pounding, nausea/vomiting (rare), photophobia/phonophobia/osmophobia, photopsia, scintillating scotomas
questions.exp: Prodrome: mood disturbance, irritability, depressive symptoms; aura: zig-zag lines (m/c); headache: unilateral -> holocranial, frontotemporal, throbbing/pounding type, nausea/vomiting (rare), photophobia/phonophobia/osmophobia, photopsia (flashing lights), scintillating scotomas; postdrome: lethargy, low mood/depressed. (Book p595)

questions.q: The migraine headache stage duration printed is:
questions.exp: Headache stage duration: 4-72 hrs. (Book p595)

questions.q: The most common migraine trigger per the page, with its stated mechanism, is:
opts: Sleep deprivation - d/t serotonin-melatonin cycle disruption
questions.exp: Triggers: sleep deprivation (m/c) d/t serotonin-melatonin cycle disruption; menstruation d/t hormonal fluctuation; excess stress; traffic, climate, mosquito, henna, food etc. (Book p595)

questions.q: The common-migraine criteria require a minimum of how many attacks, lasting how long?
questions.exp: Common migraine: minimum 5 attacks lasting 4-72 hrs; characteristics (at least 2): unilateral, pulsatile, moderate to severe intensity, aggravated by routine physical activity/movement; clinical features (at least 1): nausea/vomiting (rare), photophobia/phonophobic; not attributed to another disorder. (Book p595)

questions.q: Classical-migraine aura criteria require at least how many of the listed features?
questions.exp: Classical migraine: at least 3 attacks lasting 4-72 hrs; aura - at least 3 of: gradual, duration <60 mins, reversible, headache within 60 mins of aura OR headache preceding/simultaneous with aura; not attributable to another disorder. (Book p595)

questions.q: In the pathogenesis diagram, vasoconstriction leads to which phase?
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: vascular theory - vasoconstriction -> aura, vasodilation -> headache; serotonin theory - down level of serotonin. Important pathogenic cytokine: CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide); pathway: trigeminovascular complex. (Book p595)

questions.q: The 5-HT1F agonist ('ditans') named in the serotonin-theory Rx is:
questions.exp: Serotonin theory Rx: 5-HT1b/1d agonist: triptans (DOC); 5-HT1F agonist: ditans (Lasmiditan). (Book p595)

questions.q: The other migraine-with-aura types listed here are:
opts: Ophthalmoplegic, retinal, basilar type, familial hemiplegic (Ca2+ channelopathy)
questions.exp: Other types of migraine with aura: 1. ophthalmoplegic (transient 3rd nerve palsy, involvement of pupil +); 2. retinal (unilocular visual impairment); 3. basilar type (occipital involvement, ataxia, tinnitus, vertigo); 4. familial hemiplegic migraine: Ca2+ channelopathy. (Book p596)

questions.q: The acute-attack antiemetic options printed are:
questions.exp: Acute attack - antiemetics: metoclopramide 5-10 mg/D; domperidone. (Book p596)

questions.q: The mild-migraine column of the acute treatment table lists:
opts: Paracetamol; NSAID - naproxen 550 mg BD, ibuprofen 400 mg QID
questions.exp: Treatment table - mild: paracetamol, NSAID (naproxen 550 mg BD, ibuprofen 400 mg QID); moderate to severe: triptan (5HT1b/1d agonists) - eletriptan, rizatriptan, almotriptan, sumatriptan; very severe: sumatriptan 6 mg S/C x 2 doses intranasal, zolmitriptan intranasal. (Book p596)

questions.q: The printed maxima in the moderate-to-severe column for rizatriptan and sumatriptan are:
questions.exp: Moderate to severe: rizatriptan 5-10 mg (max: 30mg); sumatriptan 50-100 mg (max: 200mg); eletriptan; almotriptan. (Book p596)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the triptan disadvantage NOT printed on the page:
opts: C/I in cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease
questions.exp: Disadvantages of triptan: C/I in cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease; efficacy depends on Tmax; ineffective in migraine with aura. Note: ergotamine -> least recurrence of migraine. (Book p596)

questions.q: The prophylaxis first-line trio printed is:
questions.exp: Prophylaxis: first line beta-blocker, valproate, topiramate; second line SNRI (venlafaxine), TCA; third line pizotifen (5-HTa antagonist), flunarizine (Ca2+ channel blocker), clonidine, candesartan. (Book p596)

questions.q: The S/E notes: topiramate and valproate carry which adverse profiles?
opts: Topiramate: weight loss, renal calculi; valproate: weight gain, liver disease, hyperammonemia, thrombocytopenia
Topiramate: weight gain, cataract; valproate: rash only
Topiramate: renal failure; valproate: aplastic anemia
questions.exp: Note S/E: topiramate - weight loss, renal calculi; valproate - weight gain, liver disease, hyperammonemia, thrombocytopenia. (Book p596)

questions.q: The newer migraine drugs and therapies printed include which CGRP antagonist?
questions.exp: Newer drugs and therapy: erenumab (CGRP antagonist), supraorbital transcutaneous stimulation, onabotulinum toxin A, greater occipital nerve block. (Book p596)

questions.q: The TAC group on this page includes which four conditions?
opts: Cluster headaches, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT, hemicrania continua
questions.exp: Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias includes: cluster headaches, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT (short-lasting unilateral neuralgic headache with conjunctival congestion and tear), hemicrania continua. (Book p597)

questions.q: The TAC feature line: short-lasting, severe, unilateral, neuralgic headache plus which requirement?
opts: At least one ipsilateral ANS symptom (conjunctival congestion/lacrimation, nasal congestion/rhinorrhoea, eyelid edema, forehead/facial sweating or flushing, ear fullness, miosis and/or ptosis)
questions.exp: Features: headache (short-lasting, severe, unilateral, neuralgic) + ipsilateral ANS symptoms; ANS symptoms at least 1: conjunctival congestion/lacrimation, nasal congestion/rhinorrhoea, eyelid edema, forehead and facial sweating, forehead and facial flushing, sensation of fullness in ear, miosis and/or ptosis. (Book p597)

questions.q: Young male, unilateral periorbital boring non-throbbing excruciating pain, nocturnal, 1-8 attacks/day for 8-10 weeks then a symptom-free period, alcohol trigger, no cutaneous trigger - which diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cluster headache: young males (M > F); unilateral periorbital non-throbbing, stabbing/boring, excruciating (most painful headache), associated with ipsilateral ANS, nocturnal; frequency 1-8 attacks/day, symptoms for 8-10 weeks followed by symptom-free period; migrainous features (photophobia may be seen); 20% chronic symptoms; trigger alcohol, no cutaneous trigger. (Book p597)

questions.q: Cluster headache attack duration per the page is:
questions.exp: Duration of attack: 15 min - 3 hours (30 mins). (Book p597)

questions.q: The cluster-management flowchart's treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Management - treatment: 100% oxygen: treatment of choice, 12-15 L/min for 10-20 mins; sumatriptan 6 mg S/C. (Book p598)

questions.q: Short-term prevention of cluster per the list names which DOC?
questions.exp: Prevention - short-term: steroid (DOC), verapamil, galcanezumab, greater occipital nerve injection; long-term: verapamil (best), topiramate, lithium. (Book p598)

questions.q: F = m, attacks 2-30 min (average 5 min), 1-30 attacks/day, ANS +, no migraine-like feature, no alcoholic trigger, no nocturnal preponderance, and indomethacin reduces attack frequency - which TAC?
questions.exp: Paroxysmal hemicrania: F = m; type throbbing/boring/stabbing; severity excruciating; 1-30 attacks/day; duration 2-30 mins (average 5 mins); ANS symptoms +; no migraine-like feature, no alcoholic trigger, no nocturnal preponderance; treatment: indomethacin (reduce frequency of attack); no effective treatment during attack. (Book p598)

questions.q: SUNCT attack duration and frequency per the page are:
questions.exp: SUNCT: M = F, unilateral, orbital or temporal pain, stabbing/throbbing, 3-200 attacks/day; duration of attack 5-240 sec; no migraine-like features; no alcohol preponderance; cutaneous trigger +, no refractory period. (Book p598)

questions.q: SUNCT management per the page is:
opts: Treatment IV lignocaine; prevention lamotrigine or topiramate
questions.exp: SUNCT management: treatment IV lignocaine; prevention lamotrigine or topiramate. (Book p598)

questions.q: Elderly female with a continuous unilateral background headache, episodic TAC, migrainous features, ANS + and response to indomethacin - which diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hemicrania continua: elderly females; continuous nature of unilateral background headache with episodic TAC; migrainous features +; ANS symptoms +; responsive to indomethacin. (Book p598)

questions.q: The investigation-of-TAC list on this page contains which three items?
opts: MRI brain, polysomnography, pituitary function test
questions.exp: Investigation of TAC: MRI brain; polysomnography; pituitary function test. (Book p599)

questions.q: F > m, 50-60 yrs, brief electric shock-like unilateral V2/V3 pain with cutaneous trigger and refractory period, no objective sensory loss - which diagnosis and its unilateral cause?
opts: Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) - compression on the superior cerebellar artery
questions.exp: Trigeminal neuralgia (00:55:15): F > m, 50-60 yrs; paroxysms of intense pain; unilateral d/t compression on superior cerebellar artery; bilateral d/t demyelination (multiple sclerosis); type brief, electric, shock-like superficial pain; tic douloureux - wincing d/t pain; maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) divisions; no objective sensory loss; cutaneous trigger +, refractory period +; investigation: specialized MRI. (Book p599)

questions.q: Trigeminal neuralgia treatment per the page, with its required pre-test, is:
opts: Carbamazepine (>> lamotrigine) after HLA B-1502 testing; subcutaneous botulinum toxin; microvascular decompression in medically refractory cases
questions.exp: Treatment: carbamazepine >> lamotrigine - HLA B-1502 tested before administration of carbamazepine; subcutaneous botulinum toxin; microvascular decompression in medical refractory cases. Note: HLA B-5801 tested before administration of allopurinol. (Book p599)

questions.q: Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia is attributed to what per the page?
questions.exp: Unilateral: d/t compression on superior cerebellar artery; bilateral: d/t demyelination (multiple sclerosis). (Book p599)

questions.q: Sudden severe short-lasting recurrent pain in the tonsil bed, throat and angle of jaw, aggravated by coughing, yawning, swallowing, associated with cardiac conduction abnormalities - which syndrome?
questions.exp: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia: aka eagle syndrome; d/t elongation of styloid process; type sudden, severe, short-lasting, recurrent bouts of pain; site tonsil bed, throat and angle of jaw; aggravation factors coughing, yawning, swallowing; associated with cardiac conduction abnormalities. (Book p599)

questions.q: Papilledema with no neurologic signs except 6th nerve paresis is interpreted on the page as:
questions.exp: Evaluation protocol: papilledema + no neurologic signs except 6th nerve paresis: false localizing sign -> CT/MRI normal -> LP -> up opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) -> MRI: BIH or IIH. Papilledema seen in: hypertension, bradycardia, bradypnoea. (Book p600)

questions.q: The LP opening-pressure threshold in the BIH evaluation protocol is:
questions.exp: LP: up opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) -> MRI: benign intracranial hypertension (BIH) or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). (Book p600)

questions.q: The modified Dandy criteria require:
opts: Seizures, focal signs, abnormal CSF, pressure >40 cm
Headache only, normal LP, abnormal MRI
Symptoms of up ICP; no localising signs except 6th nerve palsy; normal CT/MRI; LP >25 cm H2O with normal CSF biochemistry/cytology and no other explanation
questions.exp: Modified Dandy criteria: symptoms of up ICP; no localising signs except 6th nerve palsy; normal CT, MRI findings; LP opening pressure >25 cm of H2O, CSF biochemistry/cytology normal; no other explanation for raised ICP. (Book p600)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the drug NOT listed as a secondary cause of IIH:
questions.exp: Secondary causes - drugs: outdated tetracycline, nalidixic acid, NSAIDs, retinol, danazol, tamoxifen; endocrine: steroid withdrawal, growth hormone, anabolic steroid. Primary empty sella syndrome: benign intracranial hypertension, thin rim of pituitary intact. (Book p600)

questions.q: The endocrine secondary causes of IIH printed are:
opts: Steroid withdrawal, growth hormone, anabolic steroid
questions.exp: Endocrine: steroid withdrawal, growth hormone, anabolic steroid. (Book p600)

questions.q: Headache m/c, orthostatic, daily, bilateral, worse in morning, aggravated by coughing/straining with retrobulbar pain; transient visual obscurations (seconds to minutes) and pulsatile tinnitus (unilateral > bilateral) - which disorder's clinical features?
questions.exp: Clinical features - headache m/c: type orthostatic, frequency daily, bilateral, worse in morning; aggravating factors coughing, straining; associated with retrobulbar pain. Visual symptoms: transient visual obscuration (2nd m/c), blackouts/grayouts, duration seconds to minutes, unilateral/bilateral. Tinnitus: 3rd m/c, pulsatile, heard in silent surroundings, unilateral > bilateral. (Book p601)

questions.q: The BIH treatment list marks which drug as DOC and which procedure as the best option?
opts: Mannitol (DOC); optic nerve sheath fenestration the best
Acetazolamide (DOC); repeated lumbar puncture (up to 20-30 ml) the best option
questions.exp: Treatment: weight loss; acetazolamide (DOC); topiramate; repeated lumbar puncture (upto 20-30 ml): best option; surgery - optic nerve sheath fenestrations, shunting. (Book p601)

questions.q: The acute raised-ICP note lists which five steps?
opts: Elevate head, mannitol, sedation, hyperventilation, pressor therapy to maintain CPP >60 mmHg
Head-down, dexamethasone, intubation, hyperventilation, CPP >70 mmHg
Elevate head, LP, acetazolamide, topiramate, pressors
questions.exp: Mx of acute up ICP: 1. elevate head; 2. mannitol; 3. sedation; 4. hyperventilation; 5. pressor therapy to maintain CPP >60 mmHg. (Book p601)
